subtype: Approach: rushing to finish before the deadline [Pitfall]
passage:
Two weeks before: The science teacher announced that models were due on the 15th. Vaibhav drew a quick volcano sketch and shoved it in his bag. His sister Uma started her own model that same weekend.
The night of the 14th: At nine o'clock Vaibhav remembered. He glued cardboard walls together, pasted on layers of wet newspaper and painted it brown while everything was still soaked. The glue shone. "It'll dry by morning," he said, and went to bed at midnight.
The 15th: In the morning the walls had slumped outward and the paper hung in soggy flaps. In the auto, one side fell off completely. Vaibhav carried the pieces into class in a plastic bag, and his ears burned when the teacher asked what had happened.

qa.q: When were the models due?
qa.a: On the 15th.

qa.q: What do Vaibhav's burning ears suggest?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed, carrying his model in pieces into class.

qa.q: What would you change first in Vaibhav's plan?
qa.a: Starting early, as Uma did, so there are a few days left for glue and paint to dry before the due date.

qa.q: How might Uma see Vaibhav's night-before rush?
qa.a: Uma started on the first weekend, so she might feel sorry for him but not very surprised.

grounding: Over two weeks, a boy leaves his model until the last night, glues it wet and finds it collapsed in the morning.

subtype: Approach: rushing to finish before the deadline [Pitfall]
passage: Jasleen, your project is due Friday and today is Monday? Good. Let me tell you about your Papa. When Uday was eleven, he had three weeks to make a model of the solar system. He played cricket for all three. On the last night he glued foam balls onto wires, painted them, and stuck everything onto a board at eleven o'clock. The glue was still white and wet when he went to bed. I said, "Leave it under the fan." He said, "It's fine." In the morning Saturn had slid down its wire and Jupiter was stuck to the Sun. He cried all the way to school, holding the broken board. After that, he started his projects the day he got them.

qa.q: How long did Uday have to make the model?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: How did Uday feel on the way to school?
qa.a: He cried all the way, upset and ashamed of the broken board.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story would you change?
qa.a: Spending all three weeks on cricket; starting even a few days earlier would have left time for the glue to dry.

qa.q: How might the elder have felt watching Uday that morning?
qa.a: The elder had warned about the fan and probably felt sad for him, while hoping he would learn from it.

grounding: An elder recalls a boy who rushed his model on the last night and found the wet glue had let it fall apart by morning.

subtype: Approach: following a routine of daily watering [Action]
passage: I was nine the summer I planted a tulsi and two marigolds in old ghee tins on our balcony. Bhavna-aunty from next door poked holes in the bottoms for me with a nail. The routine was simple, and I kept it the whole term: brush teeth, water plants, then school uniform. But I didn't just pour. First I pushed one finger into the soil, up to the knuckle. If it felt damp, I gave only a little. If it felt dry and crumbly, I gave a whole mug. By the monsoon the tulsi was taller than its tin, and the marigolds were little orange balls. Amma put one on the altar, and I, Parul, stood there feeling ten feet tall.

qa.q: What were the plants grown in?
qa.a: Old ghee tins.

qa.q: How did Parul feel when Amma put a marigold on the altar?
qa.a: Parul felt proud and happy, 'ten feet tall'.

qa.q: What would you change in the routine once the monsoon starts?
qa.a: Keep the finger test but expect to water less, since rain keeps the soil damp and too much water can harm the roots.

qa.q: How might Bhavna-aunty see the plants?
qa.a: Bhavna-aunty poked the drainage holes, so Bhavna-aunty would likely be pleased to see the plants thrive.

grounding: Looking back, a child describes a morning watering routine for tulsi and marigold tins, checking the soil with a finger first.

subtype: Approach: following a routine of daily watering [Action]
passage:
Eco-club note, end of July.
Kiran has taken charge of the tulsi and marigold tins on the Class 4 window ledge. Every morning she arrives ten minutes before assembly, puts her bag down and goes straight to the ledge. She does not just tip the bottle. She presses a finger into each tin first. On Monday I heard her say, "This one's still wet from Saturday, only a little." The tin nearest the fan dries faster, and she gives it more. In three weeks the marigolds have four buds. The ones in Class 5, watered "whenever", have yellowed. I have asked Kiran to show the Class 5 monitors her finger test on Friday.
Vijay, eco-club

qa.q: How many buds do the marigolds have?
qa.a: Four buds.

qa.q: What does Kiran going straight to the ledge suggest?
qa.a: She feels responsible and protective of the plants, so checking them has become part of her morning.

qa.q: What else could keep the tins healthy over a long holiday?
qa.a: She could ask a classmate or the eco-club to take turns, or move the tins away from the fan so they dry more slowly.

qa.q: What might the Class 5 monitors gain from Friday?
qa.a: Their marigolds yellowed from careless watering, so learning the finger test could save their plants.

grounding: An eco-club note shows a girl watering tulsi and marigold tins every morning before assembly after checking the soil with a finger.

subtype: Approach: finding out what each plant needs [Thinking]
passage:
Sunday
Today Nikita-didi took me to the nursery near the flyover because my chilli plant looked sad and my mint was going brown. I asked the nursery uncle why. He asked, "Where are they?" I said, "Both behind the curtain in my room." He laughed. "Chilli is a sun plant. Mint likes shade and wet feet." On the way home I thought about our flat like a map. The kitchen window gets sun all morning, so that's for the chilli. The balcony corner beside the wall stays shady and cool, so that's for the mint. I moved both pots as soon as we got home. I'll check in a week to see if I was right.
Divyansh

qa.q: Where did Divyansh put the chilli?
qa.a: By the kitchen window, which gets sun all morning.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel about the plants before the visit?
qa.a: Divyansh was worried that the chilli looked sad and the mint was going brown.

qa.q: What else could Divyansh do to test the new spots?
qa.a: Divyansh could note how the leaves look each day for a week, so it is clear whether the move helped.

qa.q: How might the nursery uncle see Divyansh's question?
qa.a: He laughed, amused at the curtain, but answered kindly, perhaps pleased that a child asked.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child learning what each plant needs from a nursery worker and placing the pots to match.

subtype: Approach: finding out what each plant needs [Thinking]
passage: At the Thursday haat in their kasba, Saurabh found Vijay-bhaiya's nursery stall between the bangle sellers and the potato heaps. He had two saplings in a cloth bag: a chilli from his aunt and a mint cutting from school. "Where should these go? Our courtyard is small." Vijay-bhaiya squinted at the plants. "Chilli wants sun from morning to afternoon. Mint wants shade and damp. Keep them apart." Walking home, Saurabh pictured the courtyard: the sunny patch by the tulsi platform, the cool corner by the handpump where the neem throws shade. That evening he set the chilli in a pot on the sunny side and planted the mint by the handpump, where splashes would keep it damp.

qa.a: Between the bangle sellers and the potato heaps at the Thursday haat.

qa.q: What was Saurabh thinking on the walk home?

subtype: Approach: overwatering out of eagerness [Pitfall]
passage: On their ninth-floor balcony in Gurugram, Jatin had planted six bean seeds in a plastic tray for a school project. The first two sprouts appeared on Monday. Jatin was so excited that he watered them before school, after school, after dinner and once more before bed. "More water, faster beans," he told his friend Divyansh on the phone. The tray had no holes. By the next week the soil smelled sour and stayed dark and wet. The leaves turned yellow at the edges, then the stems flopped over the side. When Jatin lifted one out, the root was brown and mushy, not white. He sat on the balcony floor holding it for a long time.

qa.q: How many bean seeds did Jatin plant?
qa.a: Six bean seeds.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he watered the beans four times a day?
qa.a: He was excited and eager, believing that more water meant faster beans.

qa.q: What else could Jatin try with new seeds?
qa.a: He could use a tray with holes and water only when a finger in the soil feels dry.

qa.q: What would change if the tray had drainage holes?
qa.a: Extra water would drain away, so the roots might have had air and not rotted so quickly.

grounding: A child overwaters seedlings out of eagerness until the roots rot and the plants yellow and droop.

subtype: Approach: overwatering out of eagerness [Pitfall]
passage:
"Rekha, you watered them again?"
"Only a little, Dadaji. Third time today."
"Third? The soil's already black."
"But they grow so slowly! More water, more growing."
Hemant bent and pressed the soil. Water oozed up round his thumb. "Look. They can't drink any more. They're drowning."
"Plants can't drown."
Five days later:
"Dadaji! The tomato leaves are yellow. And they're all bent over!"
Hemant slid a seedling out of the pot. The roots were brown and soft. "See? Roots need air too. We gave them a swimming pool."
"I only wanted them to grow fast." Rekha's lip wobbled.
"I know, beta. We'll start again. This time, the finger test first."

qa.q: How many times had Rekha watered that day?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What does Rekha's wobbling lip show?
qa.a: She felt upset and guilty that her eagerness had hurt the seedlings.

qa.q: What else could Rekha have done when growth seemed slow?
qa.a: She could have checked the soil first and measured the plants weekly, so small progress would show without extra water.

qa.q: How does Hemant respond to the mistake?
qa.a: Gently: he shows her the roots, explains why, and offers to start again with the finger test.

grounding: A child waters tomato seedlings several times a day to speed them up, and the roots rot until the leaves yellow and droop.

subtype: Approach: observing and recording growth [Action]
passage:
"Sunday again, Trisha. Hold the ruler straight."
"Why straight? It's a bean, not a building."
"Because if it's crooked, the number's wrong." Gurpreet read the scale. "Twenty-three centimetres."
"Last week?"
Gurpreet flipped the notebook. "Seventeen. Before that, fifteen. Before that, fourteen."
"So it jumped six this week. Why?"
"Hmm." Gurpreet ran a finger down the column where she had also written the weather. "Look. The big jumps come after rain. Fourteen to fifteen, no rain. Seventeen to twenty-three, rain on Wednesday and Thursday."
"So rain water's better than tap water?"
"Maybe. Or the days were cooler. I'll keep measuring and see."
Trisha grinned. "Scientist Gurpreet."

qa.q: How tall was the bean plant this Sunday?
qa.a: Twenty-three centimetres.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet seem to feel about the pattern?
qa.a: Curious and interested, and careful enough to keep measuring rather than jump to a conclusion.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet record to understand the jumps?
qa.a: How much tap water the plant gets and how sunny each week is, so she can tell whether rain or cooler days matter.

qa.q: How does Trisha see Gurpreet's method?
qa.a: Trisha teases at first, then admires it, calling Gurpreet a scientist. 😊

grounding: A girl measures her bean plant every Sunday, writes the heights down and notices it grows fastest after rain.

subtype: Approach: observing and recording growth [Action]
passage: Last year, for three months, I measured our bean plant every Sunday morning before breakfast. I'm Afreen, and my cousin Parveen said I was mad. I used my old school scale, held it against the stem from the soil to the top leaf, and wrote the number and the date at the back of my maths notebook. At first the numbers went up by one or two. Then in July there was a jump of seven centimetres in one week. I looked back and saw it had rained four days that week. The next big jump came after rain too. I showed my science teacher, and she said I had found a pattern with my own eyes. That felt better than any prize.

qa.q: How much did the plant grow in the July week?
qa.a: Seven centimetres.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel when the teacher praised the pattern?
qa.a: Afreen felt proud; it was better than any prize.

qa.q: What else could Afreen compare next time?
qa.a: A second plant watered only from the tap, to see whether rain itself makes the difference.

qa.q: How might Parveen see the notebook now?
qa.a: Parveen called it mad, but the teacher's praise might make Parveen see the point of measuring.

grounding: Looking back, a child recalls measuring a bean plant weekly, recording heights and spotting faster growth after rain.

subtype: Approach: figuring out why the plant is dying [Thinking]
passage: I'm Omkar, and I work next to Sahil in the school garden period. Last Tuesday his chilli plant had brown tips on nearly every leaf. He crouched down and said, out loud, "Not enough water? Sun too strong? Or bugs?" He pushed a finger into the soil: damp, so not water. He looked up at the sky: our bed gets shade after eleven, so probably not sun. Then he turned the leaves over one by one. Low on the stem there was a line of tiny black ants going up and down. He fetched a cup of soapy water from the garden teacher, wiped the stem and pushed the ant trail away with a stick. I don't know if he was worried, but he checked that plant every break for the rest of the week.

qa.q: What did Sahil find on the stem?
qa.a: A line of tiny black ants going up and down.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been feeling about the plant?
qa.a: He was probably worried, since he checked it every break for the rest of the week.

qa.q: What else could Sahil try if the tips keep browning?
qa.a: Ask the garden teacher and keep checking one cause at a time, the same careful way he ruled out water and sun.

qa.q: How does Omkar see Sahil's checking?
qa.a: Omkar notes each step Sahil took but admits not knowing whether Sahil was worried.

grounding: A classmate watches a boy test each possible cause of a sick plant and find ants on the stem.

subtype: Approach: figuring out why the plant is dying [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: Omkar noticed brown tips on the curry-leaf plant by the front door. His sister Avni said, "It's thirsty." Omkar wasn't sure. He wrote three questions on a sticky note: Water? Sun? Insects?
Wednesday: After school he checked the soil. Moist, not dry. He watched the pot at noon: sun for only an hour. That left one question. He borrowed Papa's reading glasses and a torch and peered at the stem. Ants, dozens of them, marching up to tiny white spots under the leaves.
Saturday: He had washed the stem with water every day and drawn a ring of chalk round the pot. The ants were gone. The new leaves came out plain green. Avni admitted, "Okay, not thirsty."

qa.q: What three questions did Omkar write?
qa.a: Water? Sun? Insects?

qa.q: Why didn't Omkar just water the plant?
qa.a: He felt unsure Avni was right and wanted to check each possible cause first.

qa.q: What else could Omkar do if the ants come back?
qa.a: Keep watching the stem and ask at a nursery about the white spots, since the ants may be visiting them.

qa.q: How does Avni's view change?
qa.a: Avni first says the plant is thirsty, and by Saturday admits it wasn't.

grounding: Over a week, a boy checks water, sun and pests in turn and finds ants causing his plant's brown tips.

subtype: Approach: making a small compost from kitchen waste [Action]
passage: Behind their house in a village near Nashik, Ayesha's Nani kept a cracked clay pot in the shade of the drumstick tree. "Bring me the peels," she said. So every evening Ayesha carried out the onion skins, potato peels and used tea leaves, and Nani showed her how to cover each layer with dry leaves from the yard. "Wet, then dry. Like a sandwich." Ayesha stirred it with a stick on Sundays. Her friend Rekha held her nose. "It'll stink!" It didn't, much. After six weeks Nani tipped the pot. The bottom was dark and crumbly and smelled like the fields after rain. They mixed it into the brinjal pots. When Rekha's father went to the market for fertiliser, Ayesha's pots didn't need any.

qa.q: What did Nani cover each layer with?
qa.a: Dry leaves from the yard.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt when Nani tipped the pot?
qa.a: Surprised and proud that peels had turned into dark, crumbly soil.

qa.q: What else could Ayesha do with the extra compost?
qa.a: Share a little with Rekha's family, so they could try it before buying fertiliser.

qa.q: How does Rekha see the compost at first?
qa.a: Rekha holds her nose, expecting it to stink.

grounding: With her grandmother's help, a girl turns kitchen peels and dry leaves into compost that feeds the plants.

subtype: Approach: making a small compost from kitchen waste [Action]
passage: In their flat in Amman, Rania's grandmother, Teta, saved every cucumber peel and eggshell in a bowl by the sink. "Not the bin," she said. "The balcony." Together they layered the scraps in an old plastic tub with torn newspaper and dry leaves Rania gathered under the street trees, and poked holes in the lid. Rania's friend Layla peeked in during the second week and made a face. By the fifth week the tub felt warm when Rania put her hand on it. By the eighth, the top was still lumpy but the bottom had turned dark and soft. Teta scooped it into the mint and tomato pots. "No shop bag this year," she said, and Rania grinned as the tomatoes came in fat and red.

qa.q: What was Rania feeling as the tomatoes came in?

qa.a: Layla peeked in and made a face, clearly unimpressed.

grounding: A girl and her grandmother layer kitchen scraps and dry leaves until the compost feeds their pots without bought fertiliser.

subtype: Approach: expecting results too soon [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday: Gurpreet planted a sunflower seed in a yogurt cup and set it on the windowsill. His friend Tarun said sunflowers grow as tall as doors.
Thursday: Nothing showed. Gurpreet couldn't stand it. He tipped the soil into his palm and found the seed. A tiny white root, thinner than a thread, was poking out. "It's working!" He pushed it back in, a little crooked, and pressed the soil down hard.
The next Thursday: Still nothing. He dug again, gently this time. The white root was brown and shrivelled. Tarun's sunflower, which Tarun had never touched, had two green leaves. Gurpreet planted a new seed and wrote WAIT on the cup in marker.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet find when he tipped out the soil on Thursday?
qa.a: A tiny white root, thinner than a thread, poking out of the seed.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel on Thursday before digging?
qa.a: He was impatient and couldn't stand waiting any longer.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet do to see roots without harming the plant?
qa.a: Grow a spare seed on wet cotton or in a clear cup, so he can watch the root without digging.

qa.q: What would change if Gurpreet had left the seed alone, like Tarun?
qa.a: It would likely have grown leaves too, as Tarun's untouched sunflower did.

grounding: Over two weeks, a boy digs up his seed too soon, kills the new root and learns to wait.

subtype: Approach: expecting results too soon [Pitfall]
passage: Charu, you've checked your seeds four times today. Sit down. When I, Mohit, was eight, my father gave me three pea seeds and a corner of our field. I planted them in the morning. That evening I was back, staring at the mud. On the third day I couldn't bear it. I dug up the middle one with my fingers. There it was, a little white tail curling out. I was so pleased I ran to show my father. He looked and said nothing. I pushed it back in. That one never came up. The other two, the ones I left alone, climbed the fence by the end of the month. Only then did my father say, "Some things you can't hurry."

qa.q: How many pea seeds did the father give?
qa.a: Three pea seeds.

qa.q: How did young Mohit feel on the third day?
qa.a: So impatient he couldn't bear it, and then pleased to see the root.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story cost Mohit a plant?
qa.a: Digging up the middle seed; leaving it alone like the other two would have let it grow.

qa.q: How might Mohit's father have felt when shown the root?
qa.a: He said nothing, perhaps already expecting it would not survive and letting the lesson come on its own.

grounding: An elder recalls digging up a seed after three days, killing its root, and learning that growth needs patience.

subtype: Approach: moving the pots after the leaves burn [Revision]
passage:
Tuesday, 3 May
My rose plant looked like chips today. I'm serious. At four o'clock the leaves on the side facing the terrace wall were brown, curled and crispy, and one snapped when I touched it. It's been so hot. Lokesh-bhaiya said it's getting the afternoon sun bouncing off the white wall. So I thought: morning sun is gentle, afternoon sun is fierce. I dragged the pot to the corner under the neighbour's awning, where it gets light but no burning afternoon. Then I collected dry neem leaves from the terrace and spread them on the soil so the water won't vanish so fast. Tomorrow evening I'll check whether the soil is still damp.
Irawati

qa.a: At four o'clock.

qa.a: Irawati was worried and a bit alarmed at the crispy leaves, and keen to fix it.

qa.q: What else could Irawati try if the leaves keep curling?
qa.a: Irawati could water early in the morning and keep checking the soil each evening, adjusting as the heat changes.

qa.q: How might Lokesh-bhaiya see the change?
qa.a: Lokesh-bhaiya pointed out the wall's reflected heat, so Lokesh-bhaiya would likely be pleased to see the idea used.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child moving a heat-burnt rose into partial shade and covering its soil with dry leaves to keep moisture.

subtype: Approach: moving the pots after the leaves burn [Revision]
passage: In the April heat of their village near Bundi, Sarita's rose, growing in a clay pot on the flat roof, suddenly looked scorched. Every afternoon the leaves at the top turned crisp and papery. Sudha-kaki, drying chillies next door, called across, "The roof is a tawa at three o'clock." Sarita crouched by the pot and touched the soil. Dry as dust, though she had watered it that morning. She watched the shadows: after lunch, the neem tree's shade crept over one corner of the courtyard. So she carried the pot down and set it where the shade fell, with light in the morning. Then she tucked a layer of dry straw round the stem. A week later, the new leaves stayed soft and green.

qa.q: What was Sarita thinking as she watched the shadows?

qa.a: Water in the evening as well, and ask Sudha-kaki which corner stays coolest.

qa.q: How might Sudha-kaki see Sarita's fix?
qa.a: Sudha-kaki gave the hint, so she would likely be pleased to see the rose recover.

subtype: Approach: sharing the work with a sibling [Action]
passage:
"Binod, I watered the chillies twice this week and you weeded nothing. Again."
"Because you were at cricket, Lakhan."
"So let's fix it. A chart." Lakhan taped a sheet to the wall by the back door. "Watering: you. Weeding: me. Tick when done."
"Why do I get watering? It's every day. Weeding is only twice a week."
"Fine. Then I also do the compost on Sundays."
"...Okay. That's fair."
Two weeks later, exams started.
"Binod, I have maths tomorrow. Can you do my weeding?"
"Only if you do my watering on Friday. That's my science day."
"Deal. Write it on the chart so Amma doesn't think I skipped."
Amma, passing, read the chart and laughed. "My two boys manage the plants better than I manage the kitchen."

qa.q: Where did Lakhan tape the chart?
qa.a: On the wall by the back door.

qa.q: Why did Binod object to watering at first?
qa.a: He felt resentful, since watering is every day and weeding only twice a week.

qa.q: What else could help the brothers during exams?
qa.a: They could ask Amma to cover one day a week in exam season, so neither has to trade jobs.

qa.q: How does Amma see the chart?
qa.a: Amma is amused and pleased, joking that her boys manage the plants better than she manages the kitchen.

grounding: Two brothers split watering and weeding on a wall chart so the work feels fair and the plants are cared for during exams.

subtype: Approach: sharing the work with a sibling [Action]
passage: Jomon and I are brothers, two years apart, and last year we nearly stopped speaking over a bed of tomatoes. I'm Nitin, the older one. I thought I did all the work; Jomon thought he did. So one Sunday we sat at the kitchen table with a big sheet of chart paper and made two columns. Watering, every evening: me. Weeding on Wednesday and Saturday, plus picking: Jomon. We stuck it on the wall and ticked it for three months. When my board exams came, Jomon took my watering for two weeks and wrote "exam swap" in the boxes. I did his weeding afterwards. The tomatoes never missed a day, and neither of us could say the other did less.

qa.q: What did Jomon write in the boxes during the exams?
qa.a: "Exam swap".

qa.q: How did Nitin feel about the work before the chart?
qa.a: Resentful, sure that he did all the work.

qa.q: What else could the brothers try to keep things fair?
qa.a: They could swap jobs every month, so each learns both tasks and neither feels stuck with the harder one.

qa.q: What was the chart like for Jomon?
qa.a: Jomon's work became visible, so he could not be accused of doing less, and he could help during Nitin's exams.

grounding: Looking back, a brother describes splitting garden jobs on a wall chart so neither felt the other did less, even in exam weeks.
